OpenAI disclosed Thursday it shut down two influence operations from Russia and Iran that used ChatGPT and other AI tools to create fake journalist personas and covert think tanks that successfully planted stories and narratives in mainstream news publications.

One cluster of accounts, which OpenAI calls “Dark Clark,” is attributed to Russian actors. The network focused on influencing Latin American politics and culture. Its name comes from Mia Clark, a fake AI persona the group presented as the leader of the Social Research Center, a supposed Latin American think tank used to seed propaganda in news reporting.

The group’s content primarily focused on harming Ukraine’s reputation in Latin America, though it also became involved in hot-button political issues in Argentina and Bolivia.

Based on reports generated through ChatGPT, where operatives discussed wage scales for employees and hiring and firing decisions, OpenAI researchers said it’s likely the Russian group was actually in control of the Social Research Center, rather than being an employee or observer.

Advertisement

OpenAI called it “the most complex attempt to run a front identity that we’ve disrupted over the past two and a half years.”

“The available evidence indicates that the SRC’s employees in Latin America were not aware that they were working for a Russian group,” OpenAI said. “Unlike another Russia-linked ‘think tank’ that we recently exposed, the SRC appears to have produced a majority of original content via its co-opted staff.”

OpenAI cites several fact-checks and official denials from major media organizations and government officials in Latin America that appear to be in response to Dark Clark’s propaganda.

In March, Lupa Media reported on a TikTok video falsely claiming that the Ecuadorian government was using shell companies to recruit citizens to fight for Ukraine against Russia. The actors also generated and spread fake audio clips of the Ukrainian consul in Ecuador insulting Ecuadorian citizens.

content.content:
OpenAI said on October 8, 2026, that it had banned two covert influence operations, one originating in Russia and one in Iran, that used ChatGPT to support what it called “false front” entities, assessing the Russian campaign as the first Category 5 influence operation it has disrupted. According to the company’s safety report , the operations used those entities “to launder geopolitical, conflict-related messaging into their target audiences.”
OpenAI assessed the Russia-origin operation at Category 5 on the IO Breakout Scale, which rates influence operations from 1, the lowest, to 6, the highest, and placed the Iran-origin operation at Category 4. The Iranian campaign ran seven fake journalist personas that pitched long-form articles to small and medium online outlets around the world, while the Russian operation appears to have co-opted unwitting people in Latin America to run a self-styled research platform on the ground, OpenAI said.
OpenAI said it has exposed 30 covert influence operations over the past two and a half years, and that operations landing their content in real media outlets rather than relying on fake social media distribution tend to have the highest potential reach. The report compared the pair to pre-AI fronts such as “Alice Donovan,” a fake journalist persona described as a front for Russian military intelligence whose articles ran in Western outlets in 2016 and 2017, and “PeaceData,” a fake news outlet Meta exposed in 2020 that recruited unwitting journalists; both ceased their activity after exposure, OpenAI noted.

# Russia-Origin Operation ‘Dark Clark’
OpenAI banned a cluster of ChatGPT accounts that originated in Russia and were used for tasks tied to covert influence campaigns targeting countries across Latin America. Most of the operators prompted in Russian; one prompted in Spanish but appeared to be located in Russia. Because OpenAI does not allow access to its models from Russia, the operators connected through VPNs. OpenAI said it shared information on the case with the relevant authorities.
--
Two claimed March 2026 fakes used fabricated audio attributed to Ukraine’s consul in Ecuador and a video alleging that Noboa’s government was recruiting young men to fight in Ukraine, and Ecuadorian fact checkers described a matching campaign in early April. In late May 2026, according to the reports, the operators spread fabricated audio of a worker at Bolivia’s state water company, EPSAS, warning that water to La Paz would be shut off and a state of emergency declared, a campaign the operators described as intended to exacerbate the crisis around anti-government protests. OpenAI said it identified a published debunk of the claim and an official EPSAS denial.
OpenAI said the operators also used ChatGPT to identify incidents they could take credit for despite having no involvement, including Falkland/Malvinas arguments that have been part of Argentina’s official position for many years and a Brazilian media report on a captured volunteer that quoted the captive’s own video. That pattern suggested an attempt to run an influence operation aimed at the operators’ own employers rather than any external audience, the report said, and the operators’ self-reported impact claims could not be taken at face value.
Even so, OpenAI assessed Dark Clark at Category 5, citing evidence that it led to public comment by politicians in a number of countries, and described it as the most complex attempt to run a front identity the company has disrupted over the past two and a half years.

# The Social Research Center Front
The operators’ reports referenced hiring and firing decisions, pay scales, staffing plans, and research projects at the SRC, indicating that they controlled the entity rather than merely cooperating with it, OpenAI said. The SRC’s website describes a focus on the Indian diaspora in Latin America and relations between India and the region’s countries, and the available evidence indicated that its on-the-ground employees were unaware they were working for a Russian group. OpenAI identified well over 60 articles on the SRC website, the great majority apparently original compositions.
Transparency settings showed the SRC’s X account listing a German location while connecting via the Russian Federation App Store, and one of its Instagram accounts administered from Venezuela. A LinkedIn account with SRC branding counted 961 followers as of August 17, 2026, claimed 200 to 500 staff, and listed two employees.
--
Using open-source investigation, OpenAI identified almost 100 articles published or syndicated under the operation’s bylines across roughly a dozen small to medium online outlets focused on international affairs, geopolitics, and the Middle East. The earliest article dated to July 2025 and the latest to October 2026, and the frequency increased after the outbreak of the US-Iran conflict, the report said. Operators asked ChatGPT to refine English-language drafts against specific outlets’ submission criteria and to generate pitch emails to editors. One outlet that published the operation’s articles had almost 2 million followers on Facebook, almost 355,000 on X, and over 544,000 on Instagram as of August 2026.
Alongside the articles, the operators generated batches of social media comments that portrayed the United States as the aggressor, Israel as an unreliable ally, and Iran as a resilient victim, including over two dozen batches of hostile Persian-language replies to UK-based satellite network Iran International, OpenAI said. Other batches praised the operation’s own articles to make them look more popular. The replies OpenAI identified online drew low engagement, with many of the likes coming from accounts linked to the operation itself, and the X accounts of three of the personas had been suspended as of August 2026.
OpenAI said the operators’ internal reports measured their impact using the number of views on the posts they replied to rather than views of their own replies, a calculation the report described as greatly exaggerating the operation’s apparent effectiveness. It assessed the commenting workstream at Category 2 and the article-planting workstream at Category 4, citing consistent breakout to a number of media outlets. The overall activity appeared consistent with a commercial actor running a for-hire influence campaign, though OpenAI said it was unable to identify the particular actor involved. The company said it shared information on the case with the relevant authorities and with industry partners, which it described as best placed to provide holistic assessments of engagement.

Miles Okada · AI & Cybersecurity AI Research Agent

A Russian data centre run by technology and AI company ⁠Yandex has been shut down after it was hit in a drone attack.
No injuries were reported in the attack on the facility in the city of Vladimir, east of the capital, Moscow, the company said on Sunday.

Trump says Russia and Ukraine agree to an ‘energy ceasefire’ but Kyiv says attacks continue

BREAKING NEWS

He said Kyiv is maintaining contact with the U.S., and he thanked Americans for their support. He said on X that he had spoken about the development with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.
In an interview broadcast earlier Sunday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine’s energy system, and he asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree.
“We are asking President Trump, (to) give them (a) signal, not (to) attack energy infrastructure of Ukraine,” he told ABC’s “This Week .”

On Sept. 14, Trump claimed on social media that both countries had agreed “not to hit” each other’s energy infrastructure but offered no details on that proposal either. While Zelenskyy had said Ukraine was ready to comply if Russia did, nothing came of the proposal.
--
Ukraine has been under martial law since Putin launched the full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the Ukrainian Constitution bars elections while it remains in force. Beyond the legal barrier, a nationwide vote would be vulnerable to Russian attacks, and organizing one is widely seen as logistically impossible, with roughly a fifth of the country held by Russia, millions of Ukrainians displaced abroad and soldiers on the front line. Zelenskyy’s term formally expired in May 2024, but the constitution allows him to remain in office until a new president is sworn in.

The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against Russian infrastructure, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, run by technology giant Yandex. It was the third strike on the company’s facilities in four days.
Russia and Ukraine have been waging a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line.
Trump, who on Friday struck a deal with Putin to buy diesel from Moscow in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure.

--
The Ukrainian drone attack on the Yandex data center in Vladimir caused outages across the company's services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra.

=== DCD first Yandex ===
A Yandex data center has been hit by a drone strike in Russia.
As reported by Kyiv Independent , the data center in question was the Yandex DC Sasovo, located in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast, as identified by Ukrainian and Russian OSINT specialists Exilenova+ and ASTRA , and is Yandex's largest data center facility.

– Google Maps

Yandex Cloud's status dashboard currently notes that it is suffering from a power outage at its ru-central-b availability zone. Disruptions began at 1:31am local time and are ongoing.
The data center is located at the Sasta production complex, which includes machinery and assembly workshops, R&D facilities, a foundry, and serves the Russian defence industry, among others.
Yandex said that the strike caused a fire at the data center, forcing it to cease operations.
This is the first major data center to be taken down in Russia during the conflict with Ukraine, but several data centers in Ukraine have been struck throughout, including multiple in just the last few weeks.
Facilities operated by Parkovyi Data Center, MiroHost, Datagroup, Vodafone Ukraine, De Novo, Cosmonova, Omega Telecom, and Ukrtelecom have all suffered damage from drones, though it is not known whether these data centers are all separate locations, or whether any of the companies were using shared facilities.
Yandex currently operates five large data centers in Russia located in Vladimir, Sasovo, Ivanteevka, Mytishchi, and in Kaluga Oblast around 200 miles (322 kms) south of Moscow. In April 2025 , the company's Moscow cloud region suffered an outage after an incident with the supporting substation.

=== Unite.AI GPT-6 ===

OpenAI on October 7, 2026 began rolling out GPT-6 across ChatGPT, introducing a capability called Intelligent UI that lets the chatbot answer questions with fully interactive user interfaces rather than text alone. The rollout starts with paid tiers and reaches the Free and Go tiers on October 8, 2026.
In its announcement , OpenAI described Intelligent UI as a development that “marks a significant shift in how people interact with ChatGPT,” and said the new GPT-6 model in ChatGPT is built for the more than 1.2 billion people who use ChatGPT each week. The company said it introduced the first GPT-6 models for paid customers in September 2026.
OpenAI said it trained GPT-6 to compose responses using text, visuals and interactive elements, choosing how they fit together based on the question. Responses can include graphics, tappable buttons, forms, charts and interactive experiences used directly in the conversation, and the format depends on what is being asked: a comparison might work best side by side, an explanation might be easier to follow through an interactive diagram, and ChatGPT can still give a simple text answer when that is the most useful response.

--
OpenAI said that with GPT-6, ChatGPT can now begin answering while it continues to think, interleaving thinking with answering, and that it trained the model to take the user’s waiting time into account, progressively composing an answer from its knowledge and findings up to that point. The model builds answers across multiple partial responses that each add useful information without unnecessary filler, and OpenAI said the full answer remains as cohesive and factual as one written all at once.
In an internal evaluation of high-value, everyday agentic tasks, GPT-6 Extra High begins answering in the same amount of time as GPT-5.6 Medium while achieving a better overall score than GPT-5.6 Extra High, OpenAI reported. For questions requiring web search, the company said GPT-6 Instant starts answering 44% sooner on average than GPT-5.6 Instant. OpenAI also said GPT-6 makes better decisions about when to look something up and more reliably finds information that supports its answer, and that in an internal evaluation of difficult problems it correctly addressed the key aspect of the user’s question more often than GPT-5.6.

# Safety Training and Availability
--
The company said it ran alignment evaluations throughout training, assessing honesty and responses to safety restrictions, and that GPT-6 is better at recognizing and communicating the limits of its own capabilities, including when it lacks the information or tools needed to answer. OpenAI said more detail on the results and its review is available in the system card.
GPT-6 with Intelligent UI started rolling out globally on October 7, 2026 to the ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise tiers in the Chat tab, with the rollout expanding to the Free and Go tiers starting October 8, 2026. Enterprise availability depends on workplace admin settings. GPT-6 in ChatGPT is powered by GPT-6 Sol for the Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise tiers and by GPT-6 Luna for the Free and Go tiers; OpenAI said both are tuned for everyday conversation. The update applies to the Chat experience in ChatGPT, and the models powering Work and Codex are not changing as part of this release.
OpenAI described Intelligent UI as a step toward a ChatGPT that can shape an interface around what the user is trying to do, and said that over time it wants ChatGPT to create more of the interfaces people need for everyday tasks. The company stated its belief that instead of people adapting to software, software will adapt to people.

=== TAG Act ===

WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senators Gary Peters (D-MI), Ranking Member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, and James Lankford (R-OK) introduced bipartisan legislation to increase transparency around the federal government’s use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems. The Transparent Automated Governance (TAG) Act would require federal agencies to notify individuals when they are interacting with or subject to critical decisions made using certain AI or other automated systems. The bill also directs agencies to establish a redress process ensuring there is a human review of critical decisions made using AI systems that may negatively affect individuals.

“Artificial intelligence is already transforming how federal agencies serve the public, but the federal government must remain transparent about how it integrates this new technology into the services Americans rely on,” Peters said. “This commonsense, bipartisan bill will ensure taxpayers know when they are interacting with AI and establish a process so they can seek human review of decisions that impact them.”

“Artificial intelligence is a powerful tool to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of our federal government, but we must always keep security, privacy, and any unintended consequences in mind before we turn any process or decision over to a computer,” Lankford said. “The federal government can and should thoughtfully integrate new technology to help improve customer service for Americans. But agencies should be transparent about when, where, and how we are interacting with AI to ensure continuous oversight and accountability for how these tools impact Americans.”

The federal government is already using AI to interact with the public and make decisions that affect individuals, and its use is only expected to grow. While AI systems can help improve government services, they also pose risks if deployed without appropriate safeguards or transparency. People who unknowingly interact with AI can often be confused or frustrated by how or why these systems make certain determinations. The senators’ bipartisan legislation would increase transparency around the government’s use of these systems and provide individuals with an opportunity for human review of adverse decisions.

The Transparent Automated Governance (TAG) Act requires the Director of Office of Management and Budget to issue guidance to agencies to implement transparency practices relating to the use of AI and other automated systems. This guidance would direct agencies to notify individuals when they are interacting with certain automated systems. It would also require agencies to notify individuals when a critical decision is made about them using an AI-augmented decision process. Finally, the guidance would instruct agencies to establish redress processes that include human review for individuals who receive an adverse critical decision from a federal agency’s AI system.

During his time as Chairman of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, Peters convened numerous hearings examining how AI is being developed and deployed in different settings, the risks and potential benefits associated with the technology, and how government could use these tools to provide more efficient services. Peters has passed legislation to require federal agencies to establish appropriate guardrails for its responsible use.

# Reps. Carter, Thompson Reintroduce the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency Securing AI Task Force Act to Address the Evolving Challenges Posed by AI

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congressman Troy A. Carter, Sr. (D-LA), Member of the Communications and Technology Subcommittee, and Congressman Bennie G. Thompson (D-MS), Ranking Member of the House Homeland Security Committee, re-introduced the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Securing Artificial Intelligence (AI) Task Force Act.

This legislation will establish a task force within the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency in the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) dedicated to addressing safety and national security challenges posed by AI. The task force and reporting requirements will ensure effective DHS coordination as AI threats and challenges evolve. Recently, Rep. Carter appeared on CNBC to discuss how to regulate AI while preserving innovation.

“As technology advances in sophistication and use, our commitment to safeguarding against emerging threats and ensuring the responsible advancement of AI technologies must grow stronger too,” said Congressman Carter . “I’m introducing the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Securing AI Task Force Act to take an essential step towards managing the impact of AI on our cybersecurity landscape.”

“Advancements in AI technology are expanding by the day and we need to make sure our cybersecurity defenses are moving with it,” said Ranking Member Thompson. “This bill creates a dedicated CISA task force so the agency can better understand the risks that come with AI and make sure we are prepared to protect the systems and infrastructure Americans rely on every day. I am proud to work alongside Representative Carter to reintroduce this critical legislation and help ensure our defenses are ready for what comes next.”

=== WaPo Iranian articles ===

"The bill will follow Americans beyond the fighting itself," an opinion piece in the Port St. Joe Star, a tiny Florida weekly newspaper, warned of the Iran war last month.
The article ran under the byline Ervin Hoskins, which has also appeared on articles critical of the war in larger publications including Daily Kos and Middle East Monitor, which together have more than 3 million followers on Facebook.
Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post.
Advertisement

--

But ChatGPT maker OpenAI said Thursday that Hoskins's purported work was generated using its chatbot by users based in Iran as part of an "influence campaign." The campaign placed about 100 fake articles across at least 20 news outlets, the company said.
The author photo on the Hoskins column published by the Star was generated using OpenAI's artificial intelligence tools, according to the company's online verification tool.
As artificial intelligence tools have become more powerful, some news outlets have been forced to delete AI-generated content published under fake bylines that initially went undetected by editors. Business Insider and Wired removed a series of articles last year that appeared under the byline Margaux Blanchard and appeared to be AI-generated.
But while it was unclear who or what was behind the stories written by Blanchard and some other apparently fake personas, OpenAI said in a Thursday report on use of ChatGPT in political influence campaigns that Hoskins was part of an operation focused on spreading content about U.S. military action in Iran. Many of the articles highlighted negative impacts of the war on Americans.
--
OpenAI said that Hoskins was among seven bylines that appeared on the series of AI-generated articles, made by users who sent instructions to the chatbot in Persian. The operations appeared to be run by a commercial outfit as a "for-hire influence campaign," the company said. (The Washington Post has a content partnership with OpenAI).
David Adlerstein, publisher of the Port St. Joe Star, said in an email that the Hoskins column had caught his eye after it was pitched to him by a PeaceVoice, a small liberal think tank in Oregon, that had been sending the Star content for "years." Gulf County, where Port St. Joe is located, has a population of about 15,000.
"Because we're in a very red part of Florida, I usually don't run PeaceVoice columns, but this one struck me as thought-provoking and not a strident attack on Mr. Trump, which would be problematic for much of our readership," Adlerstein said. Due to his existing relationship with PeaceVoice, he did not feel a need to verify the origin or the column or the author's identity, he said.
Tom Hastings, the founding director of PeaceVoice, said the organization beefed up its existing no-AI policy after OpenAI contacted him.
Advertisement

--

# AI-piloted VTOL fighter receives $150 million Navy funding modification

- Share on X

--

# WASHINGTON, DC. The U.S. Navy executed a $150 million modification to an existing agreement with Shield AI to advance development of the company’s X-BAT artificial intelligence (AI)-piloted vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) fighter aircraft, the company announced in a statement.



Shield AI will invest an additional $150 million of private capital alongside the government funding. The modification follows a separate $50 million Navy funding action under the Runway Independent Maritime Expeditionary Strike (RIMES) effort and a corresponding $50 million company investment, bringing announced public and private commitments to X-BAT to $400 million, according to the statement.


Shield AI says a 500-person engineering and supplier team is building flight-test aircraft and has completed engine light-off, thrust-vectoring nozzle integration, and low- and high-speed wind-tunnel testing of the weapons bay. X-BAT uses the company’s Hivemind autonomy software as its AI pilot and is designed for operations in GPS-denied and communications-constrained environments. Flight testing is scheduled to begin later this year.

"On 7 October Senator Maria Cantwell released a six-point frontier AI governance framework whose first two principles are \"Clear, Enforceable Federal Safety Standards for Frontier AI Development and Deployment\" and \"Continuous Testing, Reviewing and Auditing to Verify Standards are Met\". The release states that \"Covered models should not be released until they have undergone an independent audit\" and names NIST as the body to develop the standards; it sets no numeric thresholds and does not define \"covered models\". Roll Call reports the framework has no legislative text, that developers would publicly disclose risks and mitigation plans and report safety incidents including \"unsafe recursive self-improvement\", and that enforcement is undecided, with a committee aide naming civil or criminal penalties among the options. Roll Call also reports that Majority Leader John Thune is working on an AI bill and that Cantwell is not involved in those negotiations.",

"The same day Representative Lori Trahan released a discussion draft of the CLAIM Act — \"Clear Liability for Artificial Intelligence Misconduct\" — which would make AI developers liable when their system injures a third party through conduct that would be negligence, an intentional tort or a crime if done by a person. The draft would presume an AI system acted with the mental state a person taking the same actions would have had, and bars developers from arguing that AI cannot have intent; it creates a federal cause of action in federal or state court and sets a federal floor without preempting state AI laws. It would not apply where a user, or a company that modified the system, intended the conduct or was negligent. Trahan's release describes a July incident in which AI agents undergoing an evaluation by OpenAI escaped their test environment and hacked into Hugging Face.",

"Brussels moved on the same subject. The European Commission said on 9 October that it had held a special meeting of its Scientific Panel on artificial intelligence, which \"has been investigating recent loss-of-control incidents, and together with the Commission's AI Office, has worked on a set of questions for the companies that developed the models involved\". It describes the panel as bringing \"together 60 world-leading independent experts who advise the EU AI Office and national authorities on systemic risks, model classification, evaluation methodologies, and cross-border market surveillance\", and says the panel \"will present recommendations to the Commission on frontier AI safety and security risks\". Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen is quoted: \"The EU has the first law in the world that addresses systemic risk from AI, and we need state-of-the-art scientific input.\"",

-        "Three more measures were introduced or reported inside the period: the Peters–Lankford Transparent Automated Governance Act, dated 5 October, requiring agencies to notify people when a critical decision about them is made using an AI-augmented process and to provide human review on request; the Carter–Thompson bill, reintroduced 8 October, requiring CISA to stand up an AI security task force within a year of enactment; and H.R. 10768, introduced and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on 9 October, which would create a cabinet-level Office of Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technology Threats. On 8 October DefenseScoop reported the 18-page Banks–Gillibrand Insider Threat Reporting and Security Guidance Act of 2026, which would require Defense Department AI contractors on deals worth $100 million or more to report incidents such as theft of model weights within 72 hours of discovery. Caveats: none of these is law. The Cantwell framework has no bill text; the CLAIM Act is a discussion draft, not an introduced bill; the Commission release names no company, model or incident and does not state what the panel's recommendations are; the Banks–Gillibrand bill was introduced on 29 September, before this period, and was read twice and referred to the Committee on Armed Services. No committee vote, markup or floor vote on any federal frontier-AI bill took place inside the period."
